source.title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation

accepted.question_text: In ¹⁶O, is the sixth 0⁺ state at 15.1 MeV, about 700 keV above the four-α threshold, an α-particle condensate analogous to the Hoyle state, and can this be established experimentally through inelastic electromagnetic form factors and four-α coincidence measurements with invariant-mass reconstruction?
accepted.context_brief: Experimental verification of the ¹⁶O condensate candidate

evidence.quote: Theory predicts that analogues to the Hoyle state in 12C with its three α particles condensed into a common 0S orbit also should exist around the nα threshold in heavier self conjugate nuclei [1, 2, 3, 4]. We have made a prediction that the 6-th 0+ state at 15.1 MeV in 16O should be such a state [5].

Inelastic electromagnetic form factors are very much in need. The Hoyle state has very clearly been identified from a three α coincidence measurement [7], hinting to its α-gas like structure. A 4α coincidence measurement in 16O with determination of the invariant mass, would be extremely useful.
One of the most urgent issues is to verify experimentally that in 16O indeed the 15.1 MeV state is an α particle condensate state.

accepted.question_text: What cluster structures occur in ¹⁶O in the 15–18 MeV excitation-energy range, including possible excited states built on an α condensate and the known rotational band with I = 0⁺, 2⁺, 4⁺, and 6⁺ and a very large moment of inertia?
accepted.context_brief: Cluster spectrum of ¹⁶O near 15–18 MeV

evidence.quote: There are probably many states in 16O which can be interpreted as excited states out of the condensate. A conspicuous rotational band at around 17 MeV with I = 0+, 2+, 4+, and 6+ with a very large moment of inertia is well known since several decades [9]. It also has recently been reanalyzed by Freer et al. [10]. It is of great importance to study the cluster structures in the 15 - 18 MeV range in greater detail.

accepted.question_text: Which heavier self-conjugate A = 4n nuclei beyond ¹²C, such as ²⁰Ne, ²⁴Mg, ²⁸Si, or ⁴⁰Ca, possess dilute α-gas condensate states near their nα disintegration thresholds, and can experiments excite and identify them through large-amplitude breathing modes or soft Coulomb-explosion modes?
accepted.context_brief: Hoyle-like α-gas states in heavier A = 4n nuclei

evidence.quote: One may reasonably think that also 20Ne, 24Mg possess α gas states. The Ikeda threshold [11] increases fast though: 19.17 MeV for 20Ne, 28.48 MeV for 24Mg, 38.46 MeV for 28Si, etc.

If the experimenters were able to excite those nuclei into a large amplitude breathing mode, at some point surely they would cluster into a coherent state of α particles. Eventually for n = 8 - 10 α’s there will not exist a Coulomb barrier any longer and the condensate gas will start to expand coherently as a soft Coulomb explosion mode.
A dream may be to dissociate 40Ca into 10 α’s.

accepted.question_text: Can excited nuclei made of an inert core plus several α clusters, such as ³²S* = ¹⁶O + 4α or ⁵²Fe* = ⁴⁰Ca + 3α, host α-particle condensates, and what clear experimental fingerprint would verify such condensates?
accepted.context_brief: α condensates on inert nuclear cores

evidence.quote: However, the nα nuclei need not to disintegrate totally into nα’s. There may subsist a non disintegrated core, as e.g. 32S∗ = 16O + 4α, 52Fe∗ = 40Ca + 3α, etc. Such situations have been discussed by von Oertzen [14], Brenner [15], and Ogloblin [16]. Still a clear finger print of such α particle condensates on top of an inert core must be experimentally verified.

accepted.question_text: Do linear α-chain states exist as physical nuclear cluster states, and if they do, are their α clusters arranged in quasi-rigid Brink configurations with fixed inter-cluster distances or delocalized along the line as one-dimensional condensate-like systems?
accepted.context_brief: Nature of linear α-chain states

evidence.quote: However, this does not mean that the existence of linear alpha-chain structures is impossible. In fact, in the case of 12C, there are some reports that the third 0+ state around 10 MeV has 3α chain structure, although it is slightly bent away from the linear shape [19, 20]

The usual picture of the linear alpha-chain structure is expressed by the use of Brink wave function which has alpha clusters located on a line with equal inter-cluster distances. This means that Brink’s description assumes a quasi rigid body picture of the chain state.
From this knowledge, we can make the conjecture that the alpha clusters arranged on a line may move rather freely along the line instead of staying around some equilibrium points.

This result supports our conjecture that even in a linear configuration the α’s can preferably be in a condensate. In condensed matter such linear Bose condensates are called Tonks-Girardeau gases having quite particular properties [24, 25].

accepted.question_text: Does the short-range α–α repulsion remain dynamically active in a linear chain configuration of three or more α clusters, given that α clusters in such a one-dimensional condensate may behave as hard-core bosons?
accepted.context_brief: Short-range repulsion in α chains

evidence.quote: This stems from the fact that the ideal compact bosons cannot get around one another and, therefore, behave as hard core bosons. The fact that two bosons cannot be on the same spot turns them effectively into fermions.

It is well known that the α-α interaction has a rather strong short-range repulsion if the relative motion energy is not so high. Thus we need to investigate whether this short-range repulsion remains active in the linear chain configuration of three or more α’s.

accepted.question_text: In neutron-rich linear-chain nuclei such as ¹⁶C, do extra neutrons stabilize α-chain geometries while partly or completely preventing α condensation among the α clusters?
accepted.context_brief: Extra neutrons in α-chain condensation

evidence.quote: The linear chain structures probably are strongly stabilized if a couple of neutrons are added. Actually the linear chain has recently be considered by Itagaki et al. in 16C [26].

In such a case, it would be extremely interesting whether the fact that extra neutrons are between three α’s hinders condensation to be born out to some extent or even totally, see also discussion in Sec. 4.

accepted.question_text: Are α-particle ring configurations, such as a six-α ring in ²⁴Mg or an eight-α ring in ³²S, real nuclear cluster states after correcting mean-field artifacts, and when are rings more stable than chains as the number of α particles changes?
accepted.context_brief: Existence and stability of α rings

evidence.quote: At some point of low density the system preferred to break up into a ring of let’s say eight α particles for 32S. But a ring with six α’s also has been found in the same way.

However, the clustering probably is real. We have similar experience from the Hoyle state. Taking out the spurious center-of-mass (c.o.m.) motion of the individual α particles may bring down the energy to more realistic values. But their existence remains pure speculation for the moment.
Whether chains or rings are more stable is an open problem which, obviously, may depend on the number of α’s involved.

accepted.question_text: Do Hoyle-analogue cluster-gas states exist in non-self-conjugate nuclei with A ≠ 4n, for example ¹³C made of three α clusters plus one valence neutron or ¹¹B made of two α clusters plus one triton, and how do the extra neutrons or tritons alter the condensate character?
accepted.context_brief: Hoyle analogues with extra neutrons or tritons

evidence.quote: Besides the 4n nuclei, one can expect cluster-gas states composed of alpha clusters with extra neutrons (as well as deuterons and tritons etc.) around their cluster disintegrated thresholds in A 6= 4n nuclei, in which all clusters are in their respective 0S-orbits, similar to the Hoyle state with the (0Sα)3 configuration.

It is an intriguing subject to investigate whether or not Hoyle-analogue states exist in A 6= 4n nuclei, for example for the simplest cases, 13C (11B), composed of 3α’s and one valence neutron (2α’s and one t). The pertinent question is in which way the extra neutrons will influence the Hoyle state.
It is very intriguing to explore Hoyle-analogue states in A 6= 4n nuclei.

accepted.question_text: For ¹⁰Be-like systems with two α clusters and two valence neutrons, especially when the neutrons occupy a π orbit, is a fixed-cluster Brink wave function or a delocalized Tohsaki-Horiuchi-Schuck-Röpke (THSR) wave function more appropriate for a gas-like Hoyle analogue, and can the extra neutrons themselves occupy loosely bound 0S orbits without strongly disturbing α condensation?
accepted.context_brief: Wave-function description of neutron-rich Hoyle analogues

evidence.quote: We now have some doubt about this common picture of linear alpha-chain structure on the basis of our experience with the investigation of alpha-condensate-like states expressed by the THSR (Tohsaki-Horiuchi-Schuck-Röpke)
Let us consider the case of 10Be when the two neutrons are in a π orbit, see Fig. 2. For example is a Brink type wave function more adequate for a gas-like state than

a THSR wave function? Or, on the contrary, can we expect that such novel Hoyle-like states have in addition to the α particles also the extra neutrons in loosely bound 0S-orbits, not influencing very much the condensates?

accepted.question_text: Can nuclear structures that are stabilized by adding many neutrons to Hoyle-like, chain, or ring configurations still exhibit α-condensation aspects, despite Pauli-principle effects that may hinder formation of Hoyle-like states?
accepted.context_brief: Many-neutron effects on α condensation

evidence.quote: Generally speaking one can expect that adding a lot of neutrons to Hoyle like states will hinder their formation because of the Pauli principle. In chains and rings, as discussed before, neutron pairs between the α particle links may substantially stabilize those configurations. However, it is not clear whether these structures still show α condensation aspects.

accepted.question_text: In compact-star matter or infinite nuclear matter with non-negligible α-particle mass fractions at certain density, temperature, and asymmetry ranges, do the α particles form a condensate?
accepted.context_brief: α condensation in compact-star matter

evidence.quote: The cluster composition of compact stars is another field where eventually condensation of α particles may play a role. Recent calculations [36, 37, 38] investigate the α particle content of infinite nuclear matter as a function of density, asymmetry, and temperature. Non-negligible α particle mass fractions are found in certain parameter ranges [39]. The question then arises whether in these phases the α’s also form a condensate.

accepted.question_text: What is the correct critical temperature Tᶜα for α-particle condensation in infinite nuclear matter across both weak-coupling and strong-cluster regimes, and how can one construct a density-dependent interpolation for quartet condensation analogous to the Nozières–Schmitt-Rink scheme for pairing?
accepted.context_brief: Critical temperature for quartet condensation

evidence.quote: Quite high values for Tα c were obtained. However, the Thouless criterion applies for weak coupling situations and not for the strong coupling case with well established bosonic clusters. Therefore, the high Tα c values obtained in Ref. [40] are questionable.
What is needed is an interpolation formula covering for quartet condensation the density dependence of Tα c from high (weak coupling) to very low and vanishing densities.

In the case of pairing such an interpolation scheme between strong and weak coupling has been proposed by Nozières and Schmitt-Rink [41]. It would be very important to generalize this scheme to the quartet case.
A correct determination of the critical temperature for α particle condensation in infinite matter is also very important in the astrophysical context.

accepted.question_text: How do α particles disappear with increasing density through the Mott transition, and how does ordinary deuteron-channel Cooper pairing emerge as the more stable high-density superfluid phase?
accepted.context_brief: Mott transition from α condensation to pairing

evidence.quote: In this context another interesting problem to solve is the transition, i.e. disappearance of α particles with increasing density (Mott transition) and appearance of ordinary superfluidity (Cooper pairing in the deuteron channel). The latter being more stable at high density [40, 42].

accepted.question_text: For infinite α matter made of freely moving α particles, what first-principles calculation with full antisymmetrization of the nucleon wave function can determine the low-density symmetric-matter energy per nucleon, the α-pair distribution function, and the density-dependent modification of the α form factor?
accepted.context_brief: First-principles calculation of α matter

evidence.quote: The full calculation for α matter (freely moving α particles) would give the energy per nucleon for symmetric matter in the low-density limit. Furthermore, it would be of importance to calculate the α-pair distribution function in infinite matter, and to calculate the modification of the α form factor at increasing nucleon density within such a first principle approach that includes the full antisymmetrization of the nucleon wave function.

accepted.question_text: How should low-temperature, low-density nuclear-matter equation-of-state calculations incorporate the α–α virial coefficient and quantum condensate formation, which previous equation-of-state treatments had not yet included?
accepted.context_brief: Low-density EOS with α interactions and condensates

evidence.quote: A more detailed investigation of the internal energy should also include the virial coefficient for α − α interaction [43, 44] as well as the formation of a condensate [50] what has not been considered up to now in the EOS at low temperatures and low densities.

accepted.question_text: How can the cluster mean-field approximation be improved to include α matter correctly and to describe both the formation of quartet quantum condensates and their disappearance as density increases?
accepted.context_brief: Cluster mean-field treatment of quartetting

evidence.quote: The approximation of the uncorrelated medium can be improved considering the cluster mean-field approximation [51, 52, 53]. This would also improve the correct inclusion of α matter as discussed here. The formation of quantum condensates (quartetting) and its disappearance with increasing density demands further investigations.

accepted.question_text: For nuclear-matter equation-of-state models, how should contributions from heavier clusters with mass number A > 4 be incorporated beyond treatments that include only light clusters with A ≤ 4?
accepted.context_brief: Heavier clusters in the nuclear-matter EOS

evidence.quote: We considered only the formation of light clusters A ≤ 4. This limits the parameter range of the total neutron density ntot n , the total proton density ntot p , and T in the phase diagram to that area where the abundances of heavier clusters are small. For a more general approach to the EOS which takes also the contribution of heavier cluster into account, see Refs. [52, 54]. Future work on the nuclear matter EOS will include the contribution of the heavier clusters.

accepted.question_text: Near the density region where α bound states dissolve, does the nucleon chemical potential increase with nucleon density, indicating metastability, and what would such metastability imply for low-density nuclei?
accepted.context_brief: Metastability near cluster dissolution

evidence.quote: At present, it is unclear whether the chemical potential becomes larger with increasing nucleon density near the region, where the bound states are dissolved, indicating a region of metastability. This would be of high interest for the metastability of low-density nuclei.

accepted.question_text: How does the existence of an α-particle condensate affect nuclear-matter transport properties and reaction rates, including neutrino absorption?
accepted.context_brief: Transport and reaction-rate effects of condensates

evidence.quote: The existence of a condensate will influence not only the EOS of nuclear matter, but also the transport properties and reaction rates (e.g. neutrino absorption) in such systems.

accepted.question_text: In systems of interacting α particles, should condensation be described as condensation of individual α particles or as condensation of ⁸Be dimers or molecules, especially when Coulomb repulsion is screened in compact stars or partly screened in an α gas?
accepted.context_brief: α condensation versus ⁸Be condensation

evidence.quote: In Bose-Einstein condensation for bosons with attractive interaction the question was discussed [55] whether the bosons condense as singles or as molecules if the interaction is strong enough to bind two bosons to a molecule in free space.
Without Coulomb repulsion 8Be would be bound by 3-5 MeV. In compact stars Coulomb is screened by electrons. Even in nuclei within a gas of nα’s the Coulomb repulsion between two α’s

may be screened to some extent. It is intriguing that some studies of the Hoyle state show [19, 20] that in the loosely bound α gas state always two of the three α’s are slightly closer to one another than to the third α particle. So the question certainly is relevant whether one should consider the condensation of α’s or the one of 8Be’s.

accepted.question_text: Under what temperature, asymmetry, and time-scale conditions do heavier bosonic clusters from ¹⁶O through ⁵⁶Fe form in α-rich matter, and when should they be considered together with α and ⁸Be clusters?
accepted.context_brief: Formation of heavier bosonic clusters

evidence.quote: Of course, depending on temperature and/or asymmetry, also heavier bosonic clusters as 16O, · · ·, 56Fe can be formed. However, for the moment we do not consider this possibility, since the time scale to form these heavier clusters may be considerably longer than for the lighter ones. On the other hand, depending on temperature and/or asymmetry they may not be formed at all, see Sec. 5. Since 8Be is a loosely bound dimer of two α’s, it may be appropriate to consider both clusters together.

accepted.question_text: How do three-fermion clusters such as nucleons or tritons dissolve into their constituents at higher density or temperature, and can neutron-rich α gases form resonant gases of n tritons described by an antisymmetrized trimer product wave function?
accepted.context_brief: Gas of trimer clusters

evidence.quote: For example nucleons are in first approximation strongly bound clusters of three quarks. Then at higher densities and/or temperatures it would be very interesting to know how these clusters dissolve into their constituents, or the other way round, a process known as hadronization.
A gas of nα particles where 2n neutrons are added may have a resonant state of n tritons. Formally such a gas of trimers again could be treated with a THSR wave function [56],
The antisymmetrizer will take care of the fact that the new gas of trimers builds up its proper Fermi surface.

accepted.question_text: Can cold-atom experiments fabricate quartet condensates using four different fermion species, and do bi-excitons in semiconductors constitute quartets?
accepted.context_brief: Quartets in cold atoms and semiconductors

evidence.quote: On the other hand, the formation of cluster condensation is discussed in cold atom physics, as experimenters are able to trap simultaneously more than two kinds of fermions. For example, one has succeeded to fabricate trions [59] with three different fermions and in the future eventually also quartets with four different fermions. Whether quartets exist in the form of bi-excitons in semi conductors is still an open question [60].
